title: Creating, developing & maintaining a team
blurb: Explain how a project manager creates, develops, maintains and leads a team, and the factors that help or hinder each stage.
question: A rail operator's depot upgrade has an 18-month linear life cycle. Specialists join and leave by phase, the lead engineer resigns in month nine and the team works night shifts during the peak. What must the project manager do to create, develop and maintain an effective team, and what factors will shape each stage?

teach.h: A team is built, not found
teach.body: Team management covers the whole life of a project team: CREATING it (selecting people for skills and roles, agreeing objectives and ground rules), DEVELOPING it (building cohesion and capability), MAINTAINING it (sustaining performance and wellbeing, and managing changes in membership) and LEADING it, adapting your style as the team matures. In plain English: pick the right people, help them gel, keep them going, and change how you lead as they grow.

teach.h: The life of a project team

steps.label: Create
steps.sub: Select for skills and roles; agree objectives and ground rules

steps.label: Maintain
steps.sub: Sustain performance and wellbeing; manage joiners and leavers

steps.label: Release
steps.sub: Recognise the work, capture lessons, help people move on

teach.loop: Leadership runs through every stage and adapts as the team matures
teach.caption: A change in membership or a big change in scope can send a team back towards development, so maintenance is never 'done'.

teach.h: What the project manager does at each stage
head: Stage
PM's aim
Typical actions
rows: Skills and role mix, objectives, ground rules, kick-off
Team-building, pairing, training, agreeing ways of working
Feedback, recognition, workload and wellbeing checks, onboarding
Direct early, then coach, support and delegate as the team grows
teach.caption: Leadership is not a final step after the others: it is how the PM carries out all of them.

teach.body: Skip CREATION and you get skills gaps, duplicated work and arguments about who owns what. Neglect DEVELOPMENT and the team stays a set of individuals, stuck in conflict or politeness. Neglect MAINTENANCE and performance fades: burnout, sickness, people leaving and knowledge walking out of the door. Lead RIGIDLY and capable people disengage while new ones flounder. Each failure costs time, quality and money, so team management is part of delivering the project, not a 'nice to have'.

teach.caption: A large, dispersed team with unclear goals and high turnover takes longer to create and develop, and needs far more maintenance.

teach.h: Team life in linear and iterative projects

rows.label: Membership
values: Changes by phase as specialists join and leave

rows.label: Creation
values: PM selects to fit the WBS and OBS
Team forms around the backlog and product owner

rows.label: Maintenance
values: Protect stability and a sustainable pace

rows.label: Leadership
values: PM directs and co-ordinates the work

teach.caption: Linear teams often re-form at each phase, so the PM repeats creation and development. Iterative teams gain speed from staying together.

items.label: Create
items.sub: Civil, electrical and planning leads chosen; objectives and ground rules agreed at kick-off

items.label: Develop
items.sub: Joint site walks, pairing graduates with seniors, agreeing sign-off routes

items.label: Disruption
items.sub: Lead engineer resigns; night shifts begin and fatigue rises

items.label: Maintain
items.sub: Handover, replacement onboarded, rota rebalanced, wellbeing check-ins

items.label: Release
items.sub: Achievements recognised, lessons captured, people released

teach.caption: The PM's style shifts too: directive at kick-off, delegating by month six, then more hands-on again after the resignation.

teach.text: Don't mix up the two sets of names. Creation, development, maintenance and leadership describe what the PM DOES across a team's life. Forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning (Tuckman) describe how the TEAM behaves as it matures. Also watch for options that treat team-building as a one-off at kick-off: a new member or a major change can undo cohesion, so maintenance continues all the way to closure.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Creation: select for the right mix of skills and roles, set clear objectives and agree ground rules.
Development: build trust and capability through team-building, pairing, training and agreed ways of working.
Maintenance: sustain performance with feedback, recognition, workload and wellbeing checks, and manage joiners and leavers.
Leadership: adapt style as the team matures, more directive early, more delegating later.
Factors: name two or three (size, skills mix, goal clarity, culture, location, workload, stability) and say how each helps or hinders.
Team management = create, develop, maintain and lead, adapting as the team matures.
Creation sets the skills mix, objectives and ground rules; development builds cohesion and capability.
Maintenance is ongoing: performance, wellbeing and changes in membership.
Factors: team size, mix of skills, clarity of goals, leadership, culture, location, workload, stability.
Linear teams change by phase; iterative teams value stable, dedicated membership.

summary: You can now explain what a project manager does to create, develop, maintain and lead a team, and why each stage matters to delivery. You can also name the factors that influence each stage and explain how team life differs in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: Which activity belongs mainly to the CREATION of a project team?
options: Selecting people for skills and roles
Rebalancing workload after a resignation
Running a lessons-learned review at closure
Coaching members to resolve a disagreement
A.why: Creation is about forming the team: choosing people for the right mix of skills and roles, setting objectives and agreeing ground rules.

whyNot.1: Rebalancing workload after someone leaves is maintenance: sustaining performance through a change in membership.
whyNot.2: A lessons-learned review happens as the team is released at closure, not when it is created.
whyNot.3: Coaching people through disagreement is part of developing the team once it exists.

A.q: A team has worked flat out for three months to hit a launch date and two members are now on sick leave. Which aspect of team management most needs the project manager's attention?
options: Creation, by reselecting the team
Maintenance, by sustaining wellbeing
Development, by adding new skills
Release, by disbanding the team early
A.why: Maintenance means sustaining performance and wellbeing over time. Fatigue and sickness are classic signs that maintenance has been neglected.

whyNot.0: The people were not wrongly chosen; they are worn out. Reselecting would lose knowledge and add disruption.
whyNot.2: The problem is workload and wellbeing, not a missing skill.
whyNot.3: The work isn't finished, so releasing the team would not solve anything.

A.q:
Which THREE of the following are factors that influence the stages of a team's life?
1) Team size
2) Clarity of goals
3) Location of team members
4) The supplier's payment terms
options: 1, 2 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
A.why: Team size, clarity of goals and location all shape how quickly a team can be created, developed and maintained.

whyNot.0: Payment terms are a commercial matter, not a factor in how a team develops.
whyNot.1: Payment terms don't shape team development, and team size (1) is missing.
whyNot.3: Payment terms are not a team factor, and clarity of goals (2) is missing.

B.q: Complete the statement: In a linear life cycle, the project team's membership typically ___.
options: stays fixed from concept to transition
is chosen by the product owner each time box
is reset by the sponsor at every gate
changes as specialists join and leave by phase
B.why: Linear projects bring in different specialists for each phase (designers, then builders, then commissioning), so the PM repeatedly onboards and releases people.

whyNot.0: Fixed, stable membership is more typical of a dedicated iterative team.
whyNot.1: Product owners and time boxes belong to iterative working, and product owners don't select the team.
whyNot.2: Gates are decision points about the project's future, not routine resets of the team.

B.q: Why does a change in team membership halfway through a project matter to the project manager?
options: It can send the team back to an earlier stage
It removes the need for any ground rules
It means the whole team must be re-created
It passes team leadership to the sponsor
B.why: New joiners or leavers disturb established relationships and roles, so the team may slip back and need fresh development and onboarding.

whyNot.1: Ground rules matter even more when new people join; they need to learn and agree them.
whyNot.2: The PM onboards the new people and rebuilds cohesion; the whole team isn't started from scratch.
whyNot.3: Leading the team stays with the project manager; the sponsor doesn't take it over.

B.q: Which statement best describes the LEADERSHIP element of team management?
options: A final stage once the team is performing
A style that adapts as the team matures
A fixed style chosen when the team forms
A task handed to the most senior member
B.why: Leadership runs through the team's whole life, and the PM adapts it: more directive while the team is new, more supportive and delegating as it matures.

whyNot.0: Leadership is not a stage that comes last; it is how the PM carries out every stage.
whyNot.2: A fixed style ignores the team's changing maturity, which is exactly what this element warns against.
whyNot.3: Leading the team is the project manager's responsibility, not something passed to whoever is most senior.

C.q: An insurer's iterative claims-portal team has worked together for six time boxes and delivers reliably. The head of IT wants to swap two developers onto another project and replace them. What is the project manager's strongest argument against this?
options: Iterative teams may not change members
The sponsor alone may change membership
Stability protects cohesion and pace
New starters would cost the project more
C.why: Iterative teams gain much of their speed from stable, dedicated membership. Swapping people breaks established relationships and knowledge, so pace drops while the team rebuilds.

whyNot.0: There's no rule forbidding change; the issue is the cost of disruption to an established team.
whyNot.1: Membership isn't reserved to the sponsor; this misses the real reason, which is the effect on the team.
whyNot.3: Cost may or may not change; the main concern is lost cohesion, knowledge and pace.

C.q: Six weeks into a hospital refurbishment, team members still argue about who signs off drawings and two pieces of work have been done twice. Which part of team CREATION was most likely missed?
options: A social event to build relationships
A check of the risk register for threats
A tighter budget for each work package
Agreed roles, responsibilities and rules
C.why: Arguments over ownership and duplicated work point to roles, responsibilities and ground rules that were never clearly agreed when the team was created.

whyNot.0: Social events help development, but they don't settle who signs off what.
whyNot.1: The risk register manages uncertain events; it doesn't define who owns which tasks.
whyNot.2: Budgets control cost; they don't clarify roles or prevent duplicated work.

C.q: Which is NOT a typical team MAINTENANCE activity?
options: Onboarding a replacement team member
Monitoring workload and wellbeing
Recognising progress and achievements
Writing the project's business case
C.why: The business case is owned by the sponsor and justifies the investment. It has nothing to do with sustaining the team's performance.

whyNot.0: Onboarding a replacement is maintenance: managing a change in membership.
whyNot.1: Watching workload and wellbeing sustains performance, which is the heart of maintenance.
whyNot.2: Recognition keeps motivation up over time, so it is a maintenance activity.

reteach.title: Think of it like running a five-a-side football team
reteach.question: Picture a manager putting together a five-a-side team for a season. How do creating, developing, maintaining and leading the team map onto running it?

blocks.body: CREATE: pick a keeper, defenders and a striker, not five strikers, and agree when you train and who captains. DEVELOP: practise together until everyone knows where the others will be. MAINTAIN: rotate tired players, welcome a new signing when someone moves away, keep spirits up after a loss. LEAD: early on you call every play; by mid-season the team organises itself and you simply guide.

steps.label: Pick the squad
steps.sub: Balanced positions, captain, training night agreed

steps.label: Train together
steps.sub: Learn each other's game; build trust

steps.label: Keep it going
steps.sub: Rotate, welcome new signings, lift morale

blocks.caption: A new signing in March means some re-training: the team slips back a little before it gels again.

blocks.text: Five brilliant strikers is not a team. Creation is about the MIX of skills and roles, not just picking the most talented individuals.

explain.body: The PM selects people for the right mix of skills and roles, makes the objectives clear and agrees ground rules (how decisions are made, how people communicate, core hours, how conflict is raised). A kick-off meeting is the usual vehicle.

steps.label: Skills and roles
steps.sub: What mix does the work need?

steps.label: Objectives
steps.sub: What are we here to achieve?

test.q: What should a project manager agree with a new team so that members know how they will work together day to day?
options: Tolerances
Ground rules
A benefits profile
A stage gate
test.why: Ground rules set out how the team will behave and work together, for example how decisions are made and how people communicate.

whyNot.0: Tolerances are limits of delegated authority on time, cost or scope, set between sponsor and PM.
whyNot.2: A benefits profile shows when and how benefits will be realised; it isn't about team behaviour.
whyNot.3: A stage gate is a governance decision point, not an agreement on working practices.

explain.body: Development turns a set of individuals into a team: building trust, cohesion and capability. Typical actions are team-building, pairing less experienced members with experienced ones, training, and agreeing ways of working. In iterative projects, retrospectives do this every time box.

test.q: Which action is mainly about DEVELOPING a team?
options: Writing a role profile for a vacancy
Releasing members as their work ends
Pairing juniors with experienced staff
Approving the project management plan
test.why: Pairing builds capability and relationships, which is the core of team development.

whyNot.0: A role profile helps with creation (selecting people), not developing an existing team.
whyNot.1: Releasing people happens at the end of the team's life.
whyNot.3: Approving the PMP is a governance step for the sponsor, not team development.

explain.body: Maintenance keeps performance up over the long haul: feedback and recognition, watching workload and wellbeing, and managing joiners and leavers through handovers and onboarding. It never stops, because each change in membership can disturb a settled team.

test.q: A key analyst resigns halfway through a project. Which response best maintains the team's performance?
options: Ask the team to absorb the extra work
Pause the project until stage end
Leave the role vacant to save money
Plan a handover and onboard a successor
test.why: A planned handover keeps knowledge in the team, and proper onboarding helps the successor and the team settle quickly.

whyNot.0: Piling extra work onto others risks burnout, which is the opposite of maintenance.
whyNot.1: Pausing the whole project is out of proportion and delays delivery.
whyNot.2: Leaving the gap open overloads the team and loses the analyst's knowledge.

explain.body: Leadership adapts as the team matures. Eight factors influence every stage: team size, mix of skills, clarity of goals, leadership, culture, location, workload and stability. A big team has many more relationships to build, so it takes longer to gel.

test.q: Why might a very large project team take longer to develop than a small one?
options: There are many more relationships to build
Large teams cannot agree ground rules
Large teams always lack the right skills
Large teams have no need for a leader
test.why: Each extra person adds many new working relationships to build and co-ordinate, so trust and cohesion take longer to form.

whyNot.1: Large teams can and should agree ground rules; it just takes more effort.
whyNot.2: A large team may well have every skill it needs; size is not the same as a skills gap.
whyNot.3: Large teams need leadership at least as much as small ones.
